A prayer for America By Pastor Jim Hopkins The following is prayer was offered during the worship service at Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church in Oakland on July 14, the morning after an attempted assassination of former President Trump Loving God, Creator of All, from everlasting to everlasting you are God. In this space between everlasting and everlasting we are in a moment. A moment of fear, a moment of grief, a moment of shock, a moment of confusion, a moment of anger, a moment of desperation, a moment of very high anxiety. We are in a moment in which hope seems far, far away. In this moment help us to live humbly, to speak with quiet voices, to confess that we worship many false gods, gods named wealth, weaponry, party, nation and self. In this movement we pray for the grieving even as we give thanks for the brave. In this moment we would believe anew that you are a god of great transformations and magnificent reversals. We would trust afresh that you are able to take our sadness and make it joy, to take our doubt and make it hope and to take our fear and make it love. In this moment between everlasting and everlasting, you are God and we need you stay with us as, on this fresh morning, we do the serious work of living in a broken world. Amen. articles.text: Allen Carr leads Zenith New Orleans Parade Band in Piedmont parade for 15th year When Hollis Carr’s health began failing, the longtime Grand Marshal of the Zenith New Orleans Parade Band asked his son, Allen Carr, to take up the mantle. “When my dad became sick with cancer, he wanted me to join the band. So, I said I’d gladly take it over,” recalled Allen Carr. For many years Hollis had brought his kids to see their dad march in Piedmont’s 4th of July Parade. 2009 was the first year Allen Carr donned his father’s signature outfit – a magnificent tuxedo, black bow tie, red sash, dark shades and a red beaded necklace hanging down his chest with a crawdad. He completed his outfit with his father’s iconic parasol decorated with the colors of the Ghanaian flag. “The umbrella was a gift from a family friend, which my dad adopted for his wardrobe,” Alan explained. “There’s a straightthrough connection with New Orleans’s Line dance marching tradition and African celebrations. You’ll see umbrellas and parasols used heavily in both cultures.” The Zenith New Orleans Parade Band was founded in 1989 by local musician and bandleader Earl Scheelar (1929-2023). The band plays authentic New Orleans Jazz for dancers and music lovers alike and usually performs in two to three parades each year. Allen Carr, 62, grew up in a musical household. “I grew up playing jazz and classical. My dad played trombone, my mom played piano and sax, my brother played sax, I played sax and bass,” he said. articles.text: New report suggests Piedmonters could be doing more The City of Piedmont Sustainability Division has released a new report on climate action in Piedmont, which suggests that the city’s greenhouse gas emissions have remained stable or even increased in recent years. “According to the Businessas-Usual Forecast, Piedmont is not on track to meet the 2030 emissions reduction goal. Rather, the City will have an estimated excess of over 5,000 [Metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent]” reads an informational report presented to City Council. For comparison, 5000 metric tons of CO2 is equal to 560,000 gallons of gasoline in vehicle emissions. In light of this new information, officials believe that new interventions will be required to meet the city’s current climate goals, which include halving greenhouse gas emissions by 2030 and becoming carbon neutral by 2045. The Sustainability Division’s climate action update was delivered at a City Council meeting on July 1, 2024. “Together, transportation and building energy [sources] were responsible for over 96% of emissions in Piedmont,” stated Alyssa Romea, an AmeriCorps Climate Action Fellow with the City of Piedmont’s Sustainability Division. “We can also trace emissions to more specific subsectors,” they explained. “The first is passenger vehicles, which contributed 46.1% of total emissions. And then the second is residential natural gas, which contributed 41.6% of emissions.” She added that most homes rely on this form of energy by way of gas appliances like gas furnaces, gas water heaters and gas stoves. Romea identified these as “key areas” for the city’s attention. Romea also discussed the city’s plans to address these issues. When it comes to gas vehicles, “meeting these climate goals requires us to decarbonize transportation from gas passenger vehicles,” she said. This includes increasing support for the adoption of electric vehicles, lowering vehicle mileage and improving accessibility to alternative modes of transportation like public transit, biking and walking. The next part of the city’s plan is to reduce building emissions, which Romea said was mainly her department’s focus right now. To this end, the City plans to promote renewable electricity, source clean energy like wind and solar, reduce total energy use by increasing energy efficiency and “most importantly” promote the replacement of gas appliances with electric alternatives. As of May 2024, the City of Piedmont has issued 35 electrification rebates totaling almost $37,000 to encourage the adoption of heat pump hot water heaters, heat pump home heaters and electric panel upgrades. Piedmont has made significant growth in the last two decades in terms of sustainability. Since 2005, greenhouse gas emissions from activities within the City have fallen 33%. Currently, 24.7% of Piedmonters’ registered vehicles are electric or hybrid. The city adopted its first climate action plan in 2010. In 2018, the city released an updated second version called the Climate Action Plan 2.0. Both the first and second climate action plans included specific greenhouse gas emission targets. However, on July 17th, 2023, the city adopted a set of new goals to better match state and federal targets. Currently, they are to achieve municipal and community-scale carbon neutrality no later than 2045 as well as halving their total emissions by 2030. The city defines carbon neutrality as the point where all activities within city limits would generate zero emissions. The Piedmont Sustainability Division reports on the city’s climate action progress every year. The last update was given at a City Council meeting on July 17, 2023. Piedmont “not on track” to reach climate goals New report suggests Piedmonters could be doing more By Matt Simons The City of Piedmont Sustainability Division has released a new report on climate action in Piedmont, which suggests that the city’s greenhouse gas emissions have remained stable or even increased in recent years. “According to the Businessas-Usual Forecast, Piedmont is not on track to meet the 2030 emissions reduction goal. Rather, the City will have an estimated excess of over 5,000 [Metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent]” reads an informational report presented to City Council. For comparison, 5000 metric tons of CO2 is equal to 560,000 gallons of gasoline in vehicle emissions. In light of this new information, officials believe that new interventions will be required to meet the city’s current climate goals, which include halving greenhouse gas emissions by 2030 and becoming carbon neutral by 2045. The Sustainability Division’s climate action update was delivered at a City Council meeting on July 1, 2024. “Together, transportation and building energy [sources] were responsible for over 96% of emissions in Piedmont,” stated Alyssa Romea, an AmeriCorps Climate Action Fellow with the City of Piedmont’s Sustainability Division. “We can also trace emissions to more specific subsectors,” they explained. “The first is passenger vehicles, which contributed 46.1% of total emissions. And then the second is residential natural gas, which contributed 41.6% of emissions.” She added that most homes rely on this form of energy by way of gas appliances like gas furnaces, gas water heaters and gas stoves. Romea identified these as “key areas” for the city’s attention. Romea also discussed the city’s plans to address these issues. When it comes to gas vehicles, “meeting these climate goals requires us to decarbonize transportation from gas passenger vehicles,” she said. This includes increasing support for the adoption of electric vehicles, lowering vehicle mileage and improving accessibility to alternative modes of transportation like public transit, biking and walking. The next part of the city’s plan is to reduce building emissions, which Romea said was mainly her department’s focus right now. To this end, the City plans to promote renewable electricity, source clean energy like wind and solar, reduce total energy use by increasing energy efficiency and “most importantly” promote the replacement of gas appliances with electric alternatives. As of May 2024, the City of Piedmont has issued 35 electrification rebates totaling almost $37,000 to encourage the adoption of heat pump hot water heaters, heat pump home heaters and electric panel upgrades. Piedmont has made significant growth in the last two decades in terms of sustainability. Since 2005, greenhouse gas emissions from activities within the City have fallen 33%. Currently, 24.7% of Piedmonters’ registered vehicles are electric or hybrid. The city adopted its first climate action plan in 2010. In 2018, the city released an updated second version called the Climate Action Plan 2.0. Both the first and second climate action plans included specific greenhouse gas emission targets. However, on July 17th, 2023, the city adopted a set of new goals to better match state and federal targets. Currently, they are to achieve municipal and community-scale carbon neutrality no later than 2045 as well as halving their total emissions by 2030. The city defines carbon neutrality as the point where all activities within city limits would generate zero emissions. The Piedmont Sustainability Division reports on the city’s climate action progress every year. The last update was given at a City Council meeting on July 17, 2023. articles.text: California’s upcoming November ballot will ask voters to fund schools with money from Proposition 2, a bond measure that would allow the state to borrow $10 billion to help with repairs and upgrades at public schools. If it passes, California schools TK-12 and community colleges across the state could receive matching funds for a wide range of projects by issuing their own bonds. A similar proposal for $15 billion was rejected by voters in November 2020. Only 47% of voters were in favor of giving public schools this economic pool during the uncertainty of the Covid pandemic. Proposition 2 needs a simple majority and would provide $8.5 billion in facility renovations and new construction for TK-12 schools. Community colleges would receive the final $1.5 billion. To receive bond money, school districts must have a local bond of their own and then apply to the State Facilities Program for a funding match on a sliding scale up to 65% for renovations and 55% for new construction. Some school districts, especially those in dire need of repair, are getting the ball rolling now by putting out their own bonds in this same election. Piedmont schools are focused on their own parcel tax increase and are finishing large facility projects, notably Witter Field “We are not currently contemplating a bond,” said School Superintendent Jennifer Hawn. “If and when we do, we would involve the community in such a decision.” The 2016 money from the last successful school bond, has long since been spent by the state, and the state’s school repair fund is expected to hit zero by 2025. “It’s been long in coming and desperately needed by many districts,” said Association of Piedmont Teachers President Elise Marks. “Keeping school buildings running, safe and healthy is expensive.” The local tax is on the ballot because there is no dedicated funding stream for school facilities in the state. California depends on raising money from bonds. Voter-approved ballot initiatives have raised $43 billion in bonds since 1998.

articles.text: Piedmont’s school board is calling upon residents to help support a parcel tax increase of Measure H, which will appear on ballots in the November 5 election. During a June 26 board meeting board members took the final opportunity to formerly advocate for the special tax measure. The ballot language is: “To attract and retain highly qualified teachers and educational support staff and continue funding advanced academic programs, shall Piedmont Unified School District’s measure renewing the school parcel tax for 8 years be adopted at the rate of 50 cents per square foot of building improvements, providing 5 million dollars in annual school funding that can’t be taken away by the State, with independent citizen oversight and all money locally controlled.” “We are excited to get this campaign started. We think this is going to be fun, we’ve had fun so far. The committee is looking very strong,” said school board member Lindsay Thomasson. Dave Karol, a Beach school dad, is co-chairing the event with Claire Arno, the mother of high school students. Both were thanked by board members and Superintendent Hawn for helping organize the effort. Also given a spotlight for her efforts was teacher union president Elise Marks. “I just want to recognize your part, Dr. Marks, in bringing this to fruition,” said board member Cory Smegal. “It was really your urging, and the teachers urging, that got us thinking about it.” “I know some teachers were surprised that it took us so long to think about it,” admitted Smegal. Marks, on Zoom, accepted the thanks with grace. “Thank you, so much, to the school board for agreeing to put this forward. I know it was a little scary to take it on,” she said. There will be text banks, opportunities to write letters of support and other ways to get involved with the proposition come election time. PUSD will find out what letter of the alphabet their measure has been assigned, in August. School board member Ruchi Medhekar’s advice? “Vote yes on the parcel tax,” she said.

articles.text: August is the optimal time to view the annual Perseid Meteor Shower, one of the most active seasonal meteor showers. this, the Perseids will have begun — they last from July 14 through August 24 this year. But the good news is that they will peak for best viewing between midnight August 11 and just before sunrise August 12. As with every year, hundreds of Bay Area astronomy enthusiasts are expected to flock to Chabot Space & Science Center to commune with fellow “shooting star” hunters and glean some insights from Chabot astronomers and scientists, including Gerald McKeegan and Ben Burress. “Meteor particles enter the atmosphere at about 40-60 kilometers per second, causing shock heating and friction that quickly burns up the particles and ionizes the air around them,” explained McKeegan. “This produces the long bright streaks that we see as ‘shooting stars.’” They are called Perseids for a reason. “The meteor streaks form lines that extend back to a radiant point in the constellation Perseus, which will be in the north-eastern sky at midnight,” he explained. “As Earth orbits the Sun, its direction of motion in mid-August is toward the constellation Perseus. That gives the illusion that the meteors come out of Perseus, when it is actually the Earth that is plowing into the particle stream from the comet.” According to Science.com, “The Perseids are caused by Earth passing through debris — bits of ice and rock — left behind by Comet Swift-Tuttle which last passed close to Earth in 1992. The Perseids peak when Earth passes through the densest and dustiest area.” NASA predicts that viewers in dark sky locations this year can “expect to see up to 100 meteors per hour during the Perseid’s peak.” It’s interesting to note that Comet Swift-Tuttle takes 133 years to make one orbit of the Sun. It last reached perihelion (closest pass to the Sun) in 1992, so mark your calendars for its return in 2125. Last year was a good year to view the Perseids at their peak. This year, meteor-gazers will have to work a little harder, or at least stay up a little later, for best viewing to await the Moon’s setting to create less light interference. Other factors that affect viewing are the presence of clouds, fog and smoke in the air – all relatively unpredictable in the Bay Area. Plan to head up to Chabot Space & Science Center to view this year’s Perseid Meteor Shower between about 11 pm (PDT) Sunday, August 11, and 3 am Monday, August 12. According to Chabot astronomers, the meteor showers are best viewed without telescopes or even binoculars, so plan to just sit or lay back, look up and enjoy the show!

E v e n t C a l e n d a r Summer Thoughts July a good month to catch a falling star By Scott Horton August is the optimal time to view the annual Perseid Meteor Shower, one of the most active seasonal meteor showers. By the time you are reading this, the Perseids will have begun — they last from July 14 through August 24 this year. But the good news is that they will peak for best viewing between midnight August 11 and just before sunrise August 12. As with every year, hundreds of Bay Area astronomy enthusiasts are expected to flock to Chabot Space & Science Center to commune with fellow “shooting star” hunters and glean some insights from Chabot astronomers and scientists, including Gerald McKeegan and Ben Burress. “Meteor particles enter the atmosphere at about 40-60 kilometers per second, causing shock heating and friction that quickly burns up the particles and ionizes the air around them,” explained McKeegan. “This produces the long bright streaks that we see as ‘shooting stars.’” They are called Perseids for a reason. “The meteor streaks form lines that extend back to a radiant point in the constellation Perseus, which will be in the north-eastern sky at midnight,” he explained. “As Earth orbits the Sun, its direction of motion in mid-August is toward the constellation Perseus. That gives the illusion that the meteors come out of Perseus, when it is actually the Earth that is plowing into the particle stream from the comet.” According to Science.com, “The Perseids are caused by Earth passing through debris — bits of ice and rock — left behind by Comet Swift-Tuttle which last passed close to Earth in 1992. The Perseids peak when Earth passes through the densest and dustiest area.” NASA predicts that viewers in dark sky locations this year can “expect to see up to 100 meteors per hour during the Perseid’s peak.” It’s interesting to note that Comet Swift-Tuttle takes 133 years to make one orbit of the Sun. It last reached perihelion (closest pass to the Sun) in 1992, so mark your calendars for its return in 2125. Last year was a good year to view the Perseids at their peak. This year, meteor-gazers will have to work a little harder, or at least stay up a little later, for best viewing to await the Moon’s setting to create less light interference. Other factors that affect viewing are the presence of clouds, fog and smoke in the air – all relatively unpredictable in the Bay Area. articles.text: Piedmont Unified School District (PUSD) hosted a Summer Adventures 2024 program in June thanks in large part to the dedication and creativity of the Piedmont Unified School District (PUSD) teachers. Erin Rivera, previously of Piedmont Rec Dept. was brought on to help the district rebuild the once popular Summer Adventures, which PUSD ran for 20 years before the pandemic. Eighty eager students participated in the PUSD Summer Adventures program session at Havens. The daily offerings included a blend of academic enrichment and enjoyable activities crafted by dedicated PUSD teachers. “The teachers are the true architects of this successful initiative, leaving a lasting impact on students and educators alike,” said Rivera. This year’s program was designed not just to engage, but to educate, ensuring a holistic approach to summer learning. Each teacher poured their expertise and passion into planning engaging activities that seamlessly integrated academics with fun, creating an enriching environment for all participants. Students, including many newcomers to the district, benefited greatly from this immersive experience, setting a positive tone for their upcoming transition into the fall semester. Additionally, the Welcome to TK/Kinder, and Welcome to 6th Grade programs were specially created to help those students feel more prepared for their transition to a new school and program in the fall. These initiatives provided a supportive environment for young learners, easing their adjustment and boosting their confidence. Another cornerstone of the program’s success was the Junior Counselors-in-Training (CITs), a dedicated group of middle school students. Trained in the mornings, these young leaders showcased their skills by organizing games and activities during recess and providing crucial support to teachers in classrooms, enhancing the overall program experience. In the initial planning, over 30 PUSD teachers and staff were interested in Summer Adventures. While enrollment limitations prevented all from joining, their enthusiasm and commitment underscored the program’s value and success. Looking ahead, PUSD is committed to building upon this year’s achievements. Plans are already in motion to expand and diversify future summer programs, with expanded summer school options for all grade levels. The impact of Summer Adventures extends beyond the classroom, fostering a community of lifelong learners and setting a benchmark for innovative educational initiatives. PEBCC wins Continued from page 1 for their performances of “Salve Regina” and “Panda Chant II.” The title came with a 15-pound bronze trophy and total prize money of £1,150 (British pounds). “We didn’t expect to win,” admitted Eric Tuan, Artistic Director of the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir. Tuan, formerly a member of the choir during his youth, was also its conductor for the award-winning performance. “The competition was really stiff. Before the event, we saw that we would be competing against some of the finest youth choirs in the world – choirs from Singapore, Thailand, Canada, England, Wales, the Czech Republic – some truly outstanding choirs. So, we thought, ‘we’re just going to give our very best performance and see how we do,’” he stated. The Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir is a year-round music education and performance program for ages five through 18. It currently serves around 350 singers from the San Francisco Bay Area. In addition to competing at a high level, the choir places a special emphasis on international exchange and teaches its singers pieces from multiple countries in a variety of languages. Every summer since 1947, the Welsh town of Llangollen stages one of the world’s most inspirational and largest cultural festivals, the Llangollen Eisteddfod (literally translated to “a sitting”). Around 4,000 performers and as many as 35,000 visitors converge on this beautiful small town each year to sing and dance in a unique combination of competition, performance, and international peace and friendship. The competitions climax with the naming of the prestigious “Young Choir of the World” title, which determines the best overall choir of the event. Tensions were high before Piedmont took the stage. This was the first time Tuan had taken a team to a competition since he Photo courtesy of Llangollen International Musical Eisteddfod The Llangollen Eisteddfod’s main competitions take place at the International Pavilion, which seats up to 4,000 people. became Artistic Director in 2019. Additionally, very few students had prior competition experience because of the pandemic. “It was pretty nerve-wracking for them because they’d worked all year to prepare this repertoire,” explained Tuan. Backstage, the students listened to the choir before them perform and their anxiety grew. “One kid actually came up to me and said ‘We’re cooked,’” laughed Tuan. But when the choir stepped onstage, a profound sense of connection took hold of them. “They rose to the occasion. They gave the finest performance, certainly, that they’ve delivered all year. We worked so hard on the technique that in the moment of competition we were able to let go and abandon ourselves to the meaning of the music and to the feeling of that special connection that you have when you’re singing with each other,” recalled Tuan. The choir began their set with “Salve Regina,” a beautiful, shimmering hymn to the Virgin Mary by contemporary Basque composer Javier Busto. The tones of the Piedmont choir brought a hush over an audience of more than 1000 people. They followed with a stunning performance of “Panda Chant II,” a contemporary piece by American composer Meredith Monk. Students moved side to side and belted out sounds akin to birds and howler monkeys as they sang. “They’re moving, they’re clapping, they’re making unusual sounds in this very complicated, rhythmic way [...] it’s a joyful, animal ritual,” explained Tuan. The judges seemed to respond to their beautiful mixture of ethereal and offbeat performances. The final score was 95 – the highest of any competitors in their division. The kids of the choir gasped, cheered and hugged one another. The festival included a Celebration of Nations, where each choir proudly carried its national flag through the audience and onto the stage. After winning their division, the choir performed later that evening in a sort of grand finale. The Piedmont choir went up against winners from two other youth divisions, champions in their own right, for the title of “Young Choir of the World.” They emerged victorious. The students of the choir celebrated with shouts of joy and took photos together. Many of them were interviewed by local UK and Welsh news organizations. At the end of the competition Tuan called his mentor Bob Geary, the founding director of the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir, to tell him the good news. “He was very excited because he’s wanted us to win first place at this competition for many years, and we had finally done it. It was great to call him and acknowledge the legacy of this organization that he had created.” Tuan described the event as “one of our three greatest competitive achievements of the many competitions we’ve attended through the years.” For more information about the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir and its programs, visit https://www.piedmontchoirs.org/ programs or contact their Registrar Greg Rosas at grosas@ piedmontchoirs.org. articles.text: A novel by Chris Honoré The intended audience for the novel The Journey of Max Braverman, written by Chris Honoré, is preteens and early adolescents. The excerpt is offered as a weekly series meant to encourage reading. Hopefully, young readers will embrace the story, which focuses on the close relationship between two young brothers, Max and Jordie. The setting is a central California town called Watson in the mid-sixties. The novel can be found online at Barnes & Nobel or Amazon. PART FOUR I guess you could say that what happened, at least the beginning of what happened, started just before school let out. Just before summer vacation. And even now, looking back, I can still remember everything. But then how could I forget? My life was changed forever. It had been more than a week since Howard left, and Jordie and I said as little as possible about his being gone, afraid we’d hex it. We both hoped with all our hearts he’d never come back. But we’d turned one brick into a castle before, only to come home from school to find old Howard sitting in the family room, just off the kitchen, watching television and acting like he owned the place. We lived in a small clapboard house on the edge of Watson, a dry, dusty town in Central California. Laurel and oak trees grew in the backyard, their limbs spreading out over our house like huge umbrellas, giving shade during the long, warm summers. We grew up climbing in the trees and playing “chase the bad guys” in an open field nearby, the dense grass tall enough to hide us as we crawled back and forth, stickers getting in our hair, catching in our socks. With Howard gone, the feeling in our house changed. Things were lighter, easier somehow. Maybe it was because summer wasn’t far off. But I think it was because Howard, cranky and whiney, had declared his intention to live somewhere else, and for sure nobody was sending out any patrols to beg him to return. Our mom played the radio and hummed along as she worked in the kitchen, while Jordie and I ran in and out of the house, the screen door banging behind us. In the afternoon we’d sit at the kitchen table drinking milk and eating cookies or having a bowl of cereal with brown sugar and cold milk. And if she wasn’t working, our mom would sit with us and snap green beans into a colander or shell peas into a large white bowl or just hold a dishtowel in her hands, leaning back against the sink, asking about our day at school. Jordie and I shared a small room at the back corner of our house and we were both very particular about geography, and had this ongoing argument about my side, your side. Actually, I think we were both glad to have the company, especially on windy, rainy nights when lightning and thunderstorms rolled through Watson, gusts of wind rattling the windows, making the house creak and groan. It didn’t take much to get Jordie spooked. More than once I’d woken up to find him pushing this big overstuffed chair that filled a corner of our room, over in front of the closet door. Looking over at him, his face serious, wrestling with that old lumpy chair, I’d try not to laugh. “What the heck are you doing, Jord? It’s the middle of the damned night.” “Just give me a sec.” And saying that, he crawled into the chair, the back of it now hard up against the closet door. “Gees, Jord, you can’t sleep like that.” “Yes I can.” “Look, I can’t sleep with you sitting there like that. It’s weird. Move the chair back where it was and just get back in bed.” Jordie just sat there, his arms folded, looking at me, waiting. “Okay, fine,” I said, and got out of bed, walking over to him. “Get in bed, I’ll check the closet. Just to be on the safe side.” I slid the chair back and opened the closet door, turning on the interior light, making a show of pushing our clothes back and leaning deep inside. Then, hitting the light switch, I hustled back in bed. “Coast is clear,” I said, tunneling down under the covers. “Max, I swear, I heard something.” “It’s gone now, Jord. Could’ve been the wind. It’s blowing pretty good out there.” And it was, the leafy branches of the big tree near our bedroom window moving back and forth, brushing the side of the house. “Anyway, it’s time to get some Z’s.” And before I could even close my eyes I heard Jordie mumble, “Definitely,” already half asleep. When he slept, he was a log. We had single beds with identical blue and red-checkered bedspreads and a maple nightstand with a lamp on it in the shape of a western water pump. You moved the handle up and down to turn the light off and on. I know, pretty corny, but Jordie really liked it and always wanted to be the one to turn the light off at night, pulling down on the pump handle like he almost expected water to come shooting out of the spout. We shared one dresser, and Jordie carefully divided the drawers starting with the top one for me, alternating to the bottom. At the foot of our beds we each had an old steamer trunk made of pressed cardboard with metal hinges and locks that wouldn’t fasten. In his trunk were cigar boxes, each labeled and stacked, one on the top of the other, filled with all his found stuff. And, in one corner, right on top, where it’d be handy, was Jordie’s baseball glove, an old fielder’s mitt, the leather worn and cracked, the pocket deep and black from spit and oil and dirt. More than anything, Jordie loved that glove. Sometimes he would just sit on his bed hitting his fist into the pocket until his knuckles were all dark and grimy, fiddling with the webbing and the lacing, all the while having this sad look in his eyes. The deal was, it had belonged to our dad and even had his name, Don Braverman, written in faded black letters on the wrist strap. Post for the continued adventures of Max Braverman. In the afternoon we’d sit at the kitchen table drinking milk and eating cookies or having a bowl of cereal with brown sugar and cold milk. And if she wasn’t working, our mom would sit with us and snap green beans into a colander or shell peas into a large white bowl or just hold a dishtowel in her hands, leaning back against the sink, asking about our day at school. Jordie and I shared a small room at the back corner of our house and we were both very particular about geography, and had this ongoing argument about my side, your side. Actually, I think we were both glad to have the company, especially on windy, rainy nights when lightning and thunderstorms rolled through Watson, gusts of wind rattling the windows, making the house creak and groan. It didn’t take much to get Jordie spooked. More than once I’d woken up to find him pushing this big overstuffed chair that filled a corner of our room, over in front of the closet door. Looking over at him, his face serious, wrestling with that old lumpy chair, I’d try not to laugh. “What the heck are you doing, Jord? It’s the middle of the damned night.” “Just give me a sec.” And saying that, he crawled into the chair, the back of it now hard up against the closet door. “Gees, Jord, you can’t sleep like that.” “Yes I can.” “Look, I can’t sleep with you sitting there like that. It’s weird. Move the chair back where it was and just get back in bed.” Jordie just sat there, his arms folded, looking at me, waiting. “Okay, fine,” I said, and got out of bed, walking over to him. “Get in bed, I’ll check the closet. Just to be on the safe side.” I slid the chair back and opened the closet door, turning on the interior light, making a show of pushing our clothes back and leaning deep inside. Then, hitting the light switch, I hustled back in bed. “Coast is clear,” I said, tunneling down under the covers. “Max, I swear, I heard something.” “It’s gone now, Jord. Could’ve been the wind. It’s blowing pretty good out there.” And it was, the leafy branches of the big tree near our bedroom window moving back and forth, brushing the side of the house. “Anyway, it’s time to get some Z’s.” And before I could even close my eyes I heard Jordie mumble, “Definitely,” already half asleep. When he slept, he was a log. We had single beds with identical blue and red-checkered bedspreads and a maple nightstand with a lamp on it in the shape of a western water pump. You moved the handle up and down to turn the light off and on. I know, pretty corny, but Jordie really liked it and always wanted to be the one to turn the light off at night, pulling down on the pump handle like he almost expected water to come shooting out of the spout. We shared one dresser, and Jordie carefully divided the drawers starting with the top one for me, alternating to the bottom. At the foot of our beds we each had an old steamer trunk made of pressed cardboard with metal hinges and locks that wouldn’t fasten. In his trunk were cigar boxes, each labeled and stacked, one on the top of the other, filled with all his found stuff. And, in one corner, right on top, where it’d be handy, was Jordie’s baseball glove, an old fielder’s mitt, the leather worn and cracked, the pocket deep and black from spit and oil and dirt. More than anything, Jordie loved that glove. Sometimes he would just sit on his bed hitting his fist into the pocket until his knuckles were all dark and grimy, fiddling with the webbing and the lacing, all the while having this sad look in his eyes. The deal was, it had belonged to our dad and even had his name, Don Braverman, written in faded black letters on the wrist strap. See next week’s Piedmont Post for the continued adventures of Max Braverman. articles.text: Piedmont Fencing Team qualified five team members to the U.S. National Championships, while three competed. Pictured are Sophie Choi (left), Teresa Mckay, Oliver Greenebaum, Maya Dvoiris, and Niko Kalamas. Members of the Piedmont Fencing team competed in the National Championships in Columbus, Ohio from June 30 through July 8. He prestigious event hosts more than 6,000 of the best junior fencers in the U.S. Representing Piedmont were Piedmont High School seniors Oliver Greenebaum and Teresa McKay, along with 8th grader Maya Dvoiris. Two other members, Sophie Choi and Niko Kalamas, qualified but did not compete. “U.S. Nationals is the largest fencing tournament in the world with 6,000+ athletes competing over two weeks. This year it was in Columbus, Ohio,” said coach David Sinkkonen. “We qualified five athletes and brought three this year. We didn’t achieve the greatest results, but it’s quite an achievement to even qualify for the National Championships.” Greenebaum competed in three events, Division 2 and 3 men’s foil and junior men’s foil. In the D2 foil event on July 7, he finished 126th of 259 athletes. He had six pool matches to start, winning two matches including one against a ‘hard’ rated opponent. Oliver won one match in the Direct Elimination round, defeating Ethan Capra, but lost to Brian Kim, who finished 13th overall. Greenebaum was 126th of 259 in the D3 category on July 8. He won two of six pool matches and lost his elimination round match against ‘hard’ rated Quinn Peck, who placed 103rd. Oliver also opened the tournament on June 30 in the junior men’s foil, placing 396 of 422 athletes. “Oliver competed in three categories in the extremely difficult Jr. Men’s Foil event. Unfortunately Oliver didn’t make it out of the preliminary rounds. In DIV2 and DV3 Men’s Foil Oliver made it out of the preliminary rounds but lost early in his Direct Elimination rounds and was eliminated,” Sinkkonen said. McKay competed in the Division 1-A and Division 2 women’s foil categories. On July 3 she was 88th of 110 contestants after competing in five pool matches against ‘very hard’ or ‘hard’ rated competitors, She defeated one opponent with a ‘hard’ rating, and lost in the elimination to Anika Breker, who went on to finish 27th. Competing on July 4 in the D2 event, McKay was 145th of 179 after winning one of five pool matches, including one against ‘hard’ rated competition. Maya Divoiris (right), an 8th grader, competed in the Y-12 category at National Championships.

articles.text: The Oakland Strokes recently returned from the prestigious Rowing BC Provincial Championship Regatta at Burnaby Lake in Burnaby, British Columbia on July 12-14. They took 26 athletes and 34 boats. Each boat competed in an Open division, in addition to U17, U19, U23, Lightweight, and U23 Lightweight. Girls Results The Strokes duo of PHS junior Geneva Johnson and PHS sophomore Sophia Brenner placed 2nd in the women’s coxless 2- boat in the Under-19 division, and 5th in the open division with a time of 8:48.806. The women’s 8+ boat was third of five in its race with a time of 7:46.76. The boat included Brenner and Johnson, and Piedmont juniors Laurel Minor and Claire von Metzsch. The women’s coxed four boat with Brenner and Von Metzsch finished second of seven boats with a time of 7:49.30. Placing fourth in 8:05.67 were Johnson and PHS senior Anna Lavin. Lavin also competed in the 4x quad scull, which placed fifth of 15 boats with a time of 7:59.963. They were also third in the U19 division. Brenner was also in the 2x double scull, which placed 11th of 34 boats in 8:57.06. They were fourth of 14 boats in the U17 category. Lavin’s boat was 16th overall in 9:06.72, while von Metszch double scull was 24th in 9:36.02. In the single scull, Lavin finished 16th of 34 boats with a time of 9:58.03. The boat also placed third in the U19 division. Boys Results The Strokes’ men’s 8+ boat finished fourth in 6:36.56. It included PHS juniors Senan Brodie and Evrim Duransoy. Brodie and Duransoy also competed in the 4x quad scull, finishing 10th in the Open Division and third in the U17 division. In the single scull, Brodie won the U17 race in a field of 16 boats. He placed 18th in the open division in a crowded field of 53 boats with a time of 8:25.89. The men’s double scull was fourth 7:51.77 with Nigel Willacy and Logan Raymond. They also were second of 12 boats in the U19 category. Raymond competed in the single scull race and placed seventh in 8:03.64. Wednesday, July 17, 2024 13 Compiled by Jonathan Comeaux The summer workout series returns for its 17th year. High school athletes as well as current and former college athletes are asked how they stay in shape during the offseason. Aspiring high school and college athletes might gain some insight, as might some armchair quarterbacks. Send us suggestions of athletes you would like to see profiled in the Post this summer. Make sure you give us the person’s name, sport, phone number and e-mail address. Send your information to news@piedmont-post.com. MICHAEL AIKAWA Baseball Piedmont High Class of 2023 Lewis & Clark College Class of 2027 Portland, Oregon Michael Aikawa, PHS Class of 2023, just finished his freshman season on Lewis & Clark’s baseball team where he earned a starting role. Aikawa finished his debut collegiate season with 35 appearances and 34 starts, recording a .214 batting average with 27 hits, 10 doubles, 23 runs scored, and 18 RBIs. His best performances include going 3-for-4 with a run scored against on Puget Sound on April 13, went 2-for-3 with two doubles and three runs scored against Pacific Lutheran on April 6, and he went 4-for-5 with two RBIs and a run scored versus George Fox on March 30. He was the Post’s 2021 Sophomore of the Year and an influential four-year starter with the Highlanders. He earned second-team All-League honors as a senior and was first- team in 2022. Aikawa contributed both as a shortstop and pitcher in 2023, closing the year as the team’s leading hitter with a .357 average, 25 hits, 12 doubles, one home run, 13 RBIs and 22 runs scored. As a pitcher, he led the way with 37 innings, a 4-2 record, 44 strikeouts and a sterling 1.32 ERA, despite being a pitcher for the first time. What is your workout program this summer? Currently, my workout program with my trainer is centered around increasing my speed and agility. For example, I do exercises with pulleys as resistance and follow a chaser for my reaction time. In addition, my trainer provided me with a running program, where I run four times a week with various exercises. On the side, I have push, pull, legs, and plyometric days from exercises I collected from college programs and previous workouts. What are your fitness goals for the summer? My fitness goals for the summer are to get stronger, faster, and quicker. How are you measuring your development? I can measure strength by being able to move weight faster and being able to lift heavier weight. For speed and quickness I use a timer to see my progress. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I am working with a trainer, a hitting coach, and on my own. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? Leading Lewis & Clark in doubles my freshman year. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Don’t work without a purpose. Believe in the work that you are putting in. Believe that it is going to pay off. There are many small things that make a difference. Recently I learned that a proper amount of sleep and the quality of food I eat have become a major focus. How you fuel your body, along with your physical and mental rest is key in an athlete’s development. Piedmont High Class of 2022 University of the Pacific Class of 2026 Nico DeFazio, PHS Class of 2022, finished his redshirt freshman season at University of the Pacific in Stockton where he earned a starting role. He had a four-game hitting streak this season from March 26-30. Some of his best games include going 1-for-3 with an RBI double and a run against Seattle on February 19, 1-for-3 with an RBI and a run scored versus San Diego on March 28, and 1-for-4 with an RBI against San Diego on March 29. At Piedmont DeFazio was named the WACC Shoreline’s Player of the Year in 2022 with a .408 batting average with 29 hits, 10 doubles, three triples, and a home run. What is your workout program this summer? I am working out at Cal Strength in Danville, as well playing baseball for a summer competitive baseball team, the Walnut Creek Crawdads. I’m measuring my development through consistency and following my specific development plan through the summer. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I played in the No. 2 collegiate summer ball league with the Rochester Honkers in Minnesota, competing in the Northwoods League. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Just to continue having fun every day and to always work hard. Keep it simple. articles.text: We’re entering the final five stages of the 2024 Tour de France with Tadej Pogačar extending his lead with the Yellow Jersey through Stage 16. Since our last coverage, Pogačar has added nearly three minutes of distance between him and second place/ He is three minutes and nine seconds ahead of back-to-back champion Jonas Vingegaard. Each day, it’s looking more like Pogačar is building toward his third victory of La Grande Boucle. It hasn’t surprised many that the Slovenian Pogačar has remained in first place. Perhaps the better race is for the Green Jersey for the lead in points between Biniam Girmay and Jasper Philipsen. The Green Jersey is reserved for sprints and stage victories. Girmay currently leads with 376 points to Philipsen’s 344, both with three stage victories after Philipsen won Tuesday’s Stage 16. For Girmay, the 24-year-old Eritrean became the first cyclist of African descent to win a Tour de France stage and would make history by claiming the Green Jersey following Stage 21. All will be said and done by the time the Post writes its final story of the race. Three of the final five stages are mountain classification rides during the next week, which could be pivotal toward Pogačar solidifying the Yellow Jersey or for Vingegaard to close the gap. Photo courtesy of BicyclingMagazine.com Tadej Pogačar continues to lead the Tour de France and wear the yellow jersey of the top rider through Stage 16. Stage 17 this morning was a 177.8 km mountain stage from Saint-Paul-Trois-Châteaux to SuperDévoluy. Stage 18’s 179.5 km hilly stage that could provide another close ending between Girmay and Philipsen, and then it’s followed by two more mountain stages. Stage 19 from Embrun to Isola Ski Resort has three steep climbs with a summit finish, while Stage 20 has four categorized and another summit finish up Col de la Couillole. The Stage 21 finale on July 21 is a time trial, marking the first time Le Tour has closed on with a time trial stage since 1989. It will be a 33.7 km ride from Monaco to Nice and could make an impact in the General Classification standings, but possibly a larger effect in the battle for the Green Jersey. articles.text: The Bear Valley Music Festival will open this Sunday, July 21, marking the 55th anniversary of the iconic outdoor music festival along Highway 4. All concerts are tucked inside a large tent that holds 500 guests in the outdoor wonderland of Bear Valley, California. The festival features an eclectic variety of music from 80s tribute bands to classic jazz ensembles. “Our main goal as a nonprofit music festival is to build community and create concert events the entire Highway 4 community will enjoy. We’ve been doing it for 55 years and are excited to celebrate that milestone this summer. From the Beat to Beethoven, we’ve got something for everyone,” said Board of Directors president Julia Mee. Music Director Alexander Mickelthwate returns for his second year, and British band English Beat will open the festival with an energetic mix of musical styles, fronted by showman Dave Wakeling. English Beat fuses Latin, ska, pop, soul, reggae and punk rock and released three studio albums in the early 1980s, including I Just Can’t Stop It (1980), Wha’ppen? (1981) and Special Beat Service (1982), as well as a string of singles, including “Mirror in the Bathroom”, “Save It for Later”, “I Confess”, “Too Nice to Talk To”, “Can’t Get Used to Losing You“ and “Hands Off...She’s Mine.” Opening weekend will also include Steel ’n’ Chicago, a tribute to both Steely Dan and Chicago, and Deja Vu, a tribute to Crosby, Stills, Nash and Young. The Laurence Hobgood Trio, a Jazz ensemble, performs on Wednesday, July 26. The festival runs through Sunday, August 6. For the full festival lineup, a map and more information, visit www.bearvalleymusicfestival.org. Bear Valley Music Festival runs from July 21 to August 6. articles.text: Exhibition ends Monday Asian Art Museum in San Francisco’s exhibition Takashi Murakami: Unfamiliar People — Swelling of Monsterized Human Ego ends this Monday, July 22. Murakami: Monsterized is the first solo exhibition in San Francisco by Japanese artist Murakami, born in 1962. He is an internationally-recognized contemporary artist and major figure in global pop culture, whose influences draw from the aesthetic characteristics of the Japanese artistic tradition and the nature of postwar Japanese culture. Murakami’s influence in the contemporary art world makes his works highly sought-after in art trades and his vibrant prints maintain a consistently high value. In this exhibition, the artist’s larger-than-life paintings and sculptures use monsters, a common theme in his pieces, as a central motif. Senior Curator of Japanese Art Laura W. Allen said “the visual DNA of Murakami’s characters has origins in centuries-old styles in Japanese art, such as depicting Buddhist arhats and Daoist immortals as wizened beings with strange features, bulging eyes, and bared teeth.” Murakami adds “technicolor palette, goofy expressions, and eclectic mixture of motifs” that quickly became his trademark, Allen added. Visit https://asianart.org/ to learn more.
articles.title: Last chance to see Murakami: Monsterized at Asian Art Museum

Jones is known for her use of vivid oil pastel landscapes and exploration into Black interiority and personhood. It is the first solo museum exhibition in the United States of Jones. In this exhibition, Jones is inspired by the poetics of Black writers and the visual languages of cartoons, through her signature medium of oil pastels. The artist said she is “using motifs and color as a way to communicate ideas about the interiority of Black bodies and their lived experience.” To see all exhibitions on view, and to learn more about “Downtown First Thursdays,” visit https://www.moadsf.org/ event/free-admission-downtown-first-thursdays-2. ®

articles.text: Leonardo DiCaprio in Inception A remarkable revolution has taken place in filmmaking over the past two plus decades, one that has profoundly altered the moviegoing experience. What has occurred is the increasing use of CGI (computer generated imaging) in movies of all genres. The transformation has taken place with little fanfare, involving esoteric technology that is incorporated in even the most mundane movies without audiences taking particular note. Recent blockbusters as well as countless big tent comic book derivative films have all utilized state of the art advances in CGI hardware and software. It also has taken place with many of the recent children’s stories adapted for the screen such as “The Chronicles of Narnia,” and “Lord of the Rings.” Disney animation, where originally every frame was handdrawn and transferred to cels and then painted, is now done entirely with computers. The transition has been astonishing. What audiences see on the screen today is only limited by the imaginations of the writers, directors and cinematographers. No longer do they have to construct elaborate props, sets, handbuilt models or miniatures, or use stop-motion claymation. They can create set pieces that are mindbenders. Recall the impact of watching the groundbreaking Jurassic Park, one of the first films to effectively use CGI, replete with gripping set pieces that raised goose bumps on more than a few arms. If there’s a downside to the revolution in CGI (an estimated 50 percent of all films now use digital special effects), it has been the temptation to make special effects the main character, giving less thought to dialogue and narrative. This can turn films into carnival rides, absent of coherent stories. But when CGI is joined with exceptional storytelling, a new level of entertainment has arrived. Any discussion of CGI is mere prologue to the 2010 film Inception. Director Christopher Nolan (Dark Knight, Memento) has taken a spare story, a heist in reverse, and created a complex, visually stunning film. Set in the not too distant future, it involves a crew of corporate espionage specialists, led by Dom Cobb (Leonardo DiCaprio), who steal ideas from people’s minds while they are in a dream state. Cobb is hired for one final job by an energy mogul, Saito (Ken Wantanabe); however, instead of stealing an idea from the mind of the mark, Robert Fischer (Cillian Murphy), heir to a corporate empire, the objective will be to plant an idea in Fischer’s unconscious. If they succeed, he will decide (against his own best interest) to fragment his father’s global corporation and sell off the parts. The mission is high risk, high gain, the possibility of being lost in Fischer’s unconscious a distinct possibility. Travel into the unconscious and into a person’s dreams requires an elaborate construction of a new reality. An architect, Ariadne (Ellen Page), is brought on board to design the scenes and structure the journey. And it is in that construction that Nolan demonstrates his talent for consummate filmmaking. The movie is a labyrinth, a journey into a different world, across six countries, as the crew wends its way through multiple layers of Fisher’s unconscious, searching for the precise point where the idea can be planted (an inception as opposed to an extraction). When Fischer returns to consciousness, he will believe the suggestion is his own. Of course, the narrative, with film noir overtones, is convoluted and complicated. Despite his brilliance, Cobb has personal issues involving Mal (Marion Cotillard), his wife, and his absent children – issues which he takes along like so much personal luggage. The risk inherent in such films is that the emotional core of the movie will be lost as the special effects dazzle. And they do dazzle. But Nolan manages to sustain a coherent story throughout. It is necessary, however, to pay very close attention. Inception. Directed by Christopher Nolan. Starring Leonardo DiCaprio, Ken Wantanabe, Marian Cotillard, Ellen Page, Cillian Murphy. 2 hrs., 28 min. Rated PG-13. Released 2010. Streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv.

articles.text: A scene from Hayao Miyazaki’s The Boy and the Heron From the legendary Japanese Studio Ghibli comes the animated feature film The Boy and the Heron, written and directed by the iconic Japanese filmmaker Hayao Miyazaki. It won a 2024 Oscar, a BAFTA (British Academy of Film and Television Arts) and a Golden Globe Award. While the story is loosely based on the 1937 Japanese novel, How Do We Live, by Yoshino Genzabuno, in the main it thematically relies on the comingof-age memories of Miyazaki, as do many of his films. The story begins in Tokyo, the year is 1942, during the first months of the Pacific war. It focuses on an angry, but vulnerable 11-year-old boy, Mahito Mimaki (Luca Padovan). His mother is in a local hospital where she is killed in an allied bombing. Mahito is devastated. His father, Shoichi (Christian Bale), who works in an arms factory, makes the decision to marry his wife’s sister, Natsuko (Gemma Chan), and move the family to the countryside. Having lost his much loved mother, and weighted by grief, Mahito believes the marriage is a betrayal of his mother, and so feels a growing estrangement from his father. He also faces having to enroll in a new school where he is bullied. Unexpectedly, Mahito encounters a grey Heron (Robert Pattison) who has not only a mouth of teeth, but the ability to talk. The gravelly-voiced Heron lures Mahito to a strange, abandoned tower that is located on the estate’s property. The anthropomorphic bird claims that if Mahito goes with him, he will be reunited with his deceased mother. Of course, steeped in grief and loss, Mahito agrees, but quickly discovers that the Heron’s promise is only a mirage framed by an untruth. However, guided by the Heron, what Mahito discovers instead is that the tower has a portal to a parallel universe, one filled with strange, odd, fantastical creatures – a talking penguin (Willem Dafoe) and a parakeet king (Dave Bautista) who commands a ravenous avian army. Mahito also confronts danger, monsters and fanciful creatures. The film’s hand-drawn artistry is extraordinary and sumptuous, the tale told both tortured and whimsical, while offering a continuing contrast between the reality of loss, war and fantasy, the themes that frame The Boy and the Heron. The Boy and the Heron. Written and Directed by Hayao Miyazaki, Voiced by Mahaita Miaki, Christian Bale, Dave Bautsta, Gamma Chan. 2 hrs., 4 min. PG-13. Released in 2024. articles.text: Perhaps you have watched a television program titled McGyver. It was a series in which the hero, an incredibly resourceful and resilient young guy in a Indiana Jones leather coat and khakis, would invent his way out of impossible jams. It’s been some time since the show was on prime time television, but no matter. As it has turned out that McGyver’s name has become a verb, meaning if you can come up with a solution to a no-exit problem, fraught with clock-ticking danger, you have McGyvered it. It always involves using a combination of ad hoc stuff to include the ubiquitous duct tape. Dwayne Johnson’s most recent film Skyscraper, finds his character, Will Sawyer, in the opening scene suffering an injury that requires his retirement from the F.B.I.’s hostage rescue unit. He becomes a security specialist and has an opportunity to land a spectacular job He is able to travel with his wife, Sarah (Neve Campbell), and their two kids to Hong Kong where he will evaluate the security system of a 240- floor high-rise owned by a billionaire developer. Everything starts off peacefully until it’s not. Apparently there are some very bad people with foreign accents who, for reasons that are somewhat obscure, want to burn the building down. And so they try. It turns out that Will Sawyer’s family is staying there when the fire starts and it’s Will’s task to get inside the building – not out of the building – to rescue them. It’s something that proves to be no small thing. His situation defines high risk, high gain. Movies of this type may not be your first choice. But if you have time on a warm, slow moving day and the kids – newbie tweens, teens – are grumbling that there’s nothing to do, try the pure escapism found in Skyscraper. It’s the perfect choice. Kids love pulp cinema. Dwayne Johnson, aka The Rock, a fine specimen of a man and once an ex-wrestler, is perfectly cast. He’s managed to carve out a niche in action movies that call for brawn and good intentions. And in this film he actually pulls out a roll of duct tape and bandages a wound. McGyvered. It’s all a thrill, and the muscle-bound charisma of Johnson is evident in every frame. Skyscraper. Directed by Rawson Marshall Thurber. Starring Dwayne Johnson, Neve Campbell and Roland Moller. 1 hr., 43 min. PG-13. Released in 2018. Streaming on Fandango/prime/ hulu/apple tv. Dwayne Johnson in Skyscraper

pages.text: Wednesday, July 17, 2024 21 Features Walking on Wednesday Wednesday Walkers learn more about Piedmont’s architecture By Jim Kellogg A strong turnout of 54 walkers and three K-9 best friends was on hand for a special walk through the center of Piedmont on July 10. Architect and walker Jim Kellogg had agreed to lead the group in another discussion of Piedmont’s early 20th Century architectural development. Before they started off, thanks were given to Lois Price and Sherry Jacobs who organized the group’s participation in Piedmont’s 4th of July Parade, and the 25 walkers and K-9 who marched. The focus of Jim’s tour was the distinctive architectural character of early Piedmont. He noted that when the city was incorporated in 1907, it was a small community of only 1,700 residents and was thought of as “The Queen of the Hills.” It was a beautiful place to live and included homes with exceptional architectural character that are still appreciated today. The city’s architecture was influenced by many families from around the country who moved to Piedmont in early 1900 and wanted their new homes to recall the style from where they came. The city center provides examples of French Colonial, Victorian, English Tutor, Colonial Revival, American Foursquare, Bungalow, and Craftsman styles. By 1920, Piedmont had more than doubled in size to 4,400 residents. During the “Roaring 20s” Piedmont was referred to as “The City of Millionaires” because it had the largest number of millionaire residents per square mile of any city in America. Many of the homes reflected the success of its residents. The planned walk was two miles and would go through parts of the early city center – Bonita, Park Way, Mesa, Highland, upper Oakland, Pacific, and Mountain Avenues. It started at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, which was built in 1926 and designed by Albert Farr, then past the Jesse Wetmore House for a view from the Bonita Avenue side of this beautiful French Colonial house built in 1878. This house was restored by Alice Erskine in the 1940s and listed in the National Register of Historic Places in 1978. The Wetmore House is noted for its colonial wrap-around front porch and beautiful wood “fretwork” detailing. The tour continued on to the Rupert Whitehead House on Bonita Avenue, built in 1907. The group gathered for a photo in front of it and discussed the English Tutor style with unusual detailing which includes a stucco exterior finish and a unique double arched overhang at the front entry. Further up Bonita, the group visited several examples of houses built in a variety of styles. The first was a French-style bungalow with a pair of “oxeye windows” at the corner of Oakland Avenue, then the noteworthy Berkenfeld Victorian built in 1895, with extensive Bavarian style carved wood detailing, and the humble Craftsman shingle-style house built in the same year but with a completely different style than the Berkenfeld Victorian. The group walked to Mesa and stopped at the Lowell Hardy house, built in 1905. This house is an excellent example of Berkeley craftsman shingle-style influenced by Bernard Maybeck. The house includes a complex gable roof, projecting bay windows and sun porch, and handcrafted wood front entry. The next stop was the John Rackliffe house at the corner of Oakland and Highland Avenues, built in 1899. It is a distinctive Queen Anne shingle-style, designed with a steep multi-gable roof, distinctive “Witches Cap Turret,” wrap-around front porch, and whimsical shingle detailing. Many people do not know that an extensive second story addition was added to the house about 10 years ago, designed by Greer Graff. The scale and workmanship of the addition fits perfectly with the original house and received a Piedmont Planning Design Award. The walking group then moved on to the house next door on Oakland Avenue. This is a great example of a mid-century International Style. It was built in 1952 and is completely different from Queen Anne Victorian. The style is quiet, restrained, with an open plan layout focused on a large private backyard atrium. The architectural detailing includes full height expansive glass walls, low-slope hip roof with a raised interior ceiling below and no-frills detailing using natural materials. Which house was more appealing was left up to each member of the group to decide. The final stop on the tour was the Hugh Craig House, built in 1879. It is an excellent example of Victorian Stick Italianate, designed by Charles L. Bugbee who was a partner in San Francisco with his father, S.C. Bugbee. They had many notable clients, including Leland Stanford, Charles Crocker, Richard Tobin, and David Colton. They were the architects for Mills Hall at Mills College. The Hugh Craig House was thought to be Charles L. Bugbee’s last work, because he died in January 1880, just after the Craig House was completed. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. articles.text: Part 2 For the second year in a row, I was delighted to attend the “Taste of Sonoma” event put on by the Sonoma County Vintners Association. Just like last year this was one of the best organized and most impressive wine tastings I have ever attended. Everything was top-notch – the food trucks were amazing and varied – tacos, pizza, paella, BBQ. There were numerous comfortable seating areas where guests could relax under the shade of the trees or tents. articles.text: Myra Elizabeth Dickson, known as Liz Dickson to friends and colleagues, a well-respected realtor in Piedmont and the surrounding area, passed quietly in her home in Walnut Creek on June 9, 2024. She was 86. Born on December 10, 1938, she grew up in a small farming community with two siblings. As time went on neither of them wanted to continue farming. Liz went on to the University of Iowa and after graduating dreamed of seeing far off places. She became a flight attendant for four years with United Airlines. Jim Dickson saw her picture on the front page of the United Airlines magazine and quickly wanted to meet her. Meeting her went extremely well and six months later he proposed to her. They got married and moved to Oakland. Liz got a job in a well-known travel agency and Jim took a position with his uncle in a real estate business selling land to developers of apartment buildings. They had two boys and as time went on they joined Claremont Country Club for their youth programs and for senior tennis and golf. They enjoyed spending weekends with friends playing golf. Jim started to build apartment buildings and Liz raised their two boys. They lived in a two-story house in Oakland. Liz became interested in having a more fulfilling job and Jim arranged an appointment for Liz to join the Grubb Company, the top real estate firm at that time headed by DJ Grubb. For 30 years Liz enjoyed success as a real estate agent. As time passed and for health Well-respected realtor Liz Dickson died on June 9. reasons, they moved to a one-story home in Rossmoor Village in Walnut Creek. Liz got terminally ill due to chronic pneumonia. Liz lived a good life. She loved to read books, play golf, exercise, take walks and watch sports on tv. She was known as a strongwilled woman. She was so loved by her family and will be greatly missed. Her husband is thankful for almost 62 years of marriage and a beautiful life together and for the enduring love of their family. articles.text: Oakland Zoo prepares for moving beloved male African Elephant to Tennessee Osh during a pool day. After 20 years at the Oakland Zoo, Osh is moving to a new home at The Elephant Sanctuary in Tennessee in the fall, allowing him to be with other African elephants. Donna, the last female African elephant at the Zoo moved to the same location last September. The decision to move Osh to the Sanctuary was made after careful consideration and consultation with the AZA’s African Elephant Taxon Advisory Group (TAG). After more than a year of discussions, it was agreed that while difficult and heartbreaking, this was the best decision for the wellbeing of Osh. As an AZA-accredited facility that ensures the same gold standard of care, the availability of other possible social companions, and the decades-long relationship with Oakland Zoo, the Sanctuary provides the most suitable home for Osh for the rest of his life. “Although it’s difficult to say farewell to Osh, we’re filled with joy knowing he’s found a new home at The Sanctuary. He will have the opportunity to socialize and develop relationships with many other elephants over his lifetime. It is something that we could not offer him here. Those of us who know and love him, including our Oakland Zoo community, will miss him terribly,” said Colleen Kinzley, VP of Animal Care, Conservation and Research at the zoo. For the past year, the Zoo has worked with AZA in a nationwide Photos by Melinda Bartlett-Blante search, yet no compatible African elephants in protected care were available now or anytime soon to join Osh at Oakland Zoo. Upon his arrival in Tennessee in the fall Osh will immediately be able to communicate with and smell other elephants. Elephants often communicate using low-frequency vocalizations over many miles. Two new 3,000-square-foot bull barns are under construction for Artie, an African elephant male aged 41, and Osh at The Elephant Sanctuary. Osh will have the opportunity to get to know Artie across fence lines. After settling into the new barns and habitats, and with the care staff at The Sanctuary, Osh will also have the opportunity for introductions to African female elephants. We are hopeful that Osh and Donna will have the opportunity to reunite. Moving Osh, who weighs 15,000 pounds and stands 11 feet 2 inches tall, requires significant time and preparation to ensure his comfort during transit. He will be transported in a specially designed, air-conditioned trailer, providing enough space for the 40-hour journey to Tennessee. In the upcoming months, the Animal Care team at Oakland Zoo will hold voluntary training sessions to prepare Osh for the journey. Members of The Sanctuary’s animal care and veterinary staff will also visit Oakland Zoo to connect with his current staff and begin building their relationships with Osh. articles.text: Dear Macmama: My wife and I just updated our will and trust, but I feel like I should make other preparations. For example, should I give my passwords to my kids, so they can access my computer when I pass away? Allen P., Oakland Dear Allen: The more that you can prepare your family members for the event of your passing, the easier time they will have with the immense work involved in settling an estate. I know that most of us work hard to make sure we have all our financial affairs in order so our beneficiaries will have an easier time when we pass, but there are so many things in our digital life that we don’t think of. One of my nephews, who works in cyber security says that each person should create a digital “If I Go Missing” folder that contains all our important passwords and phone numbers. Things like our email passwords, credit card and bank passwords, airlines, shopping and Apple ID to name a few. If you just examine your daily routine, you will be amazed at how many times you must sign in or authenticate to access an account, a website, a subscription or your bank. It’s a good idea to take notes for a week or so, to determine what to add to this folder or document. Now comes the tricky part. If you have a document or a spreadsheet with all this vital information, where can you keep it securely and away from hackers or thieves? Here are a few possibilities: 1. On a piece of paper in a safe. As long as you give the combination to your home safe and let your family members know that this document is there, it’s as safe as anything in your home. Which is to say, it can be stolen or broken into, but still better than in a drawer in your desk. 2. A document on your computer. This is the most common solution and can be encrypted with a password. Again, you must let your family members know how to get into your computer and where this document is stored. But this is not the best solution, as it’s not very secure and often difficult to access when you are not present. 3. In a Google Doc. I know that many folks keep private info in a Google document, limiting access by only sharing access with family members. Google’s servers are as secure as most cloud suites, but not meant for ultra-secure data. This also has setbacks, not so much because there is a security issue, but there is too much room for user error. 4. On password management software like 1Password, or LastPass. These are my choice, since they offer the opportunity to create “family vaults”. In the case of 1Password, you can add another “family organizer” so they have access to your account in case you can’t sign in or pass away. LastPass also has levels of access that you can allow other users. What about accessing your iPhone and iPad? Apple has finally provided a new feature in the soon to be released iOS 15.2 for your iPhone and iPad, that promises help for family members trying to wrestle with your data after you are gone. As of this new update (to be released sometime soon), you will be able to add Legacy Contacts, trusted people who can access your Apple ID and your devices in the event of your death. After providing a death certificate, these contacts will be provided an access key to download all your data. Of course, this will include everything, so make sure you really trust them! As our lives become more technically involved, so must our preparation for access to this technology postmortem. And as one who has struggled to settle the estate of a loved one, and been frustrated with no access to necessary passwords for the countless accounts we had to close, I have become committed to making sure my own family will have an easier time after I am gone. Cookie Segelstein is the Macmama, an Apple Certified Service Professional that provides Apple computer consultation and trouble-shooting in your home and office. For more information, call 520-7760, email cookie@themacmama.com or visit her website at www.themacmama.com

Each of the Seniors simply stepped to a designated spot in front of the gowns, and the gowns magically appeared on them. There were three gowns available: a 1955 gown by Yves Saint Laurent, an evening ensemble with a plunging neckline by San Francisco designer Kaisik Wong and a 1987 print gown by Valentino. This was a rare opportunity for the group to envision themselves in a Valentino or other gowns by famous designers. Even the men in the group enjoyed trying them on. The current exhibition, entitled “Fashioning San Francisco: A Century of Style,” showcased a variety of gowns by designers including Christian Dior, Alexander McQueen, and John Rogers. The collection also includes designs from French couturiers, Japanese avant-garde designers, and other pillars from the fashion industry. The gowns ranged from timeless classics that are perfect for today, to those which were beautiful but more like costumes of a bygone era. Some of the gowns being exhibited have never been on display before. The exhibit includes designer shoes. The gowns are placed at different levels throughout the galleries, which give the exhibit an interesting touch. You can see how fashion evolved, starting from the 1906 earthquake, to the 21st century. There are several “basic black” dresses on display, which are still popular today, and to more formal gowns that could be worn to the San Francisco Opera or Symphony, For an extra touch, the Seniors had an audio tour so they could listen to the stories behind the exquisite gowns and move through the galleries at their own pace. The exhibit will be open to the public through August 11. To complete their outing, the Seniors ventured to the De Young Tower on the 8th floor to enjoy a fabulous panoramic view of San Francisco and the Golden Gate Bridge. And no excursion by the group would be complete without lunch, so the group enjoyed a delicious meal in the De Young Café before heading home. To find out more about the Piedmont Seniors and their activities, including monthly meetings or to receive a quarterly newsletter, contact Seniors’ Coordinator Janet Epstein at jepstein@piedmont.ca.gov.
