Importance of settling your finances By Cookie Segelstein Dear Macmama: My wife and I just updated our will and trust, but I feel like I should make other preparations. For example, should I give my passwords to my kids, so they can access my computer when I pass away? Allen P., Oakland Dear Allen: The more that you can prepare your family members for the event of your passing, the easier time they will have with the immense work involved in settling an estate. I know that most of us work hard to make sure we have all our financial affairs in order so our beneficiaries will have an easier time when we pass, but there are so many things in our digital life that we don’t think of. One of my nephews, who works in cyber security says that each person should create a digital “If I Go Missing” folder that contains all our important passwords and phone numbers. Things like our email passwords, credit card and bank passwords, airlines, shopping and Apple ID to name a few. If you just examine your daily routine, you will be amazed at how many times you must sign in or authenticate to access an account, a website, a subscription or your bank. It’s a good idea to take notes for a week or so, to determine what to add to this folder or document. Now comes the tricky part. If you have a document or a spreadsheet with all this vital information, where can you keep it securely and away from hackers or thieves? Here are a few possibilities: 1. On a piece of paper in a safe. As long as you give the combination to your home safe and let your family members know that this document is there, it’s as safe as anything in your home. Which is to say, it can be stolen or broken into, but still better than in a drawer in your desk. 2. A document on your computer. This is the most common solution and can be encrypted with a password. Again, you must let your family members know how to get into your computer and where this document is stored. But this is not the best solution, as it’s not very secure and often difficult to access when you are not present. 3. In a Google Doc. I know that many folks keep private info in a Google document, limiting access by only sharing access with family members. Google’s servers are as secure as most cloud suites, but not meant for ultra-secure data. This also has setbacks, not so much because there is a security issue, but there is too much room for user error. 4. On password management software like 1Password, or LastPass. These are my choice, since they offer the opportunity to create “family vaults”. In the case of 1Password, you can add another “family organizer” so they have access to your account in case you can’t sign in or pass away. LastPass also has levels of access that you can allow other users. What about accessing your iPhone and iPad? Apple has finally provided a new feature in the soon to be released iOS 15.2 for your iPhone and iPad, that promises help for family members trying to wrestle with your data after you are gone. As of this new update (to be released sometime soon), you will be able to add Legacy Contacts, trusted people who can access your Apple ID and your devices in the event of your death. After providing a death certificate, these contacts will be provided an access key to download all your data. Of course, this will include everything, so make sure you really trust them! As our lives become more technically involved, so must our preparation for access to this technology postmortem. And as one who has struggled to settle the estate of a loved one, and been frustrated with no access to necessary passwords for the countless accounts we had to close, I have become committed to making sure my own family will have an easier time after I am gone. articles.text: “We cannot cure the world of sorrows, but we can choose to live in joy.” – Joseph Campbel As seniors get older, they may face many challenges in life. Loss of health or loved ones can affect them deeply. While life is filled with ups and downs for all of us and we will not be happy at every moment, it is important to try and help seniors when they are experiencing sadness. Caregivers can play a crucial role in spreading joy to those in their care. Here are four ideas to assist you in bringing happiness to a senior. Encourage the use of assistive devices to maximize independence As people age, they may become less mobile and experience difficulty performing daily tasks. They might not know how to ask for help but there are many products they can use to make their life simpler and more comfortable. Reach out to your healthcare provider for a PT/OT consultation to ensure that you are using the correct devices for your particular needs. If your senior loved one is having a hard time walking, they can use a scooter or walker to help them get around. It may also be helpful to have a shower seat or grab-bars installed in their bathroom, to assist them in safely moving around the room. Seniors experiencing dexterity issues can also utilize products to make their life easier, such as an electric toothbrush. Ask for their stories Just like all of us, older adults want to know that their life has meaning. Ask them to tell you about one of their favorite memories – for example, “What did you enjoy doing most as a kid?” “Did you have a favorite pet when you were growing up?” “What has brought you the most joy in life?” It’s important to listen closely and ask relevant questions as they share details from their life. Many seniors feel like no one remembers them or that they are a burden to their loved ones. You can counteract these feelings by asking to know more about them and their past. They will feel fulfilled in sharing the favorite parts of their life journey with you. Just keep in mind that seniors may not always feel like talking and that’s okay too. Give them a chance to share if they are comfortable but don’t pressure them to have a conversation if they are not in the mood. Find classes that align with their interests Boredom is a very common occurrence amongst older adults. There are lots of classes they can take to help fill their time with enjoyable activities. Here is a list of a few that they can try: Activities for Seniors • Yoga: There are many yoga classes designed specifically for seniors. Yoga can help calm the mind and body, especially yoga exercises that are slow and gentle. Seniors with limited mobility can try doing chair yoga which will allow them to increase strength, f lexibility and breath awareness, all from a seated position. • Painting: Art is an excellent form of self-expression and a great outlet for seniors to share their experiences with the world. Studies have shown that art therapy has many benefits, both physical and mental, for seniors. Picking up a paintbrush can help seniors keep their motor skills sharp and improve hand-eye coordination. The bright, vibrant colors • can boost their mood and help reduce depression or anxiety. Painting can also assist seniors with concentration skills and memory, all while improving confidence and giving them a sense of control. Cooking: There are many cooking classes geared towards seniors which may offer advice regarding specific diets, such as making nutritious meals or meals with low salt content. These classes can be taken in-person which allows seniors to make social connections and establish friendships. Or, for the senior who has a hard time getting out or who prefers to take classes from the comfort of home, there are online options as well. Treat them with compassion When interacting with parents, grandparents and other loved ones, it’s important to remember to speak with compassion. Seniors want to know that their voice matters and that they will be treated with dignity. We should strive to always speak to seniors with care, patience, and respect, being mindful of any physical or mental challenges they are experiencing. If you can do this, you will see that your efforts go a long way in bringing joy to seniors and making them feel appreciated. pages.text: Wednesday, July 17, 2024 29 Wisteria Way Continued from page 1 owners’ application for a lot split was approved by way of ministerial approval. There was no public review process for the building design. SB 9 was passed and signed by Governor Newsom in 2021. This bill went into effect on January 1, 2022. Neighbors living nearby have taken issue with this lack of public review, criticizing what they see as a lack of transparency by the City of Piedmont and in particular a distrust of the Piedmont Planning and Building Department and its director Kevin Jackson. Neighbors insist that the project endangers protected wetlands, as defined by the US Fish and Wildlife Service, which should Contractors begin cutting down trees from a wooded area on Wistaria Way. Photo by Diane Prioleau Staff photos Harvey Lederman, a concerned citizen who lives on Wistaria Way, speaks to City Council about possible actions they could take before construction begins. Staff photos Teddy McWilliams, whose family has lived in Piedmont for over 80 years, attended the City Council meeting on Monday, July 15, in opposition to the project on Wistaria Way. Staff photos Resident David Ashton is worried about how the project will affect his property. Staff photos Councilman Tom Ramsey questions City Attorney Michelle Kenyon about whether the City can start notifying residents about SB9 applications. Photo by Diane Prioleau Workers at 77 Wistaria Way took down 14 trees on the first day of construction, according to eyewitnesses. have made the project ineligible for SB9 approval in the first place. The City and the Planning Department claim that there are no wetlands on the lot. A photo with this article shows running water in an area that feeds into Wildwood Creek. “We’re not saying they shouldn’t build. Just that they should build within what’s appropriate for our city,” said David Ashton, who lives downstream from the project. Ashton fears how the new construction will affect his own property. “Our house on Woodland Way backs right up against the property,” he explained. When Ashton became curious about how the project would affect his home, he made a public records request for the developers’ hydrology report of the area. “The report indicated that this project is going to increase runoff to downhill properties by 18%. They have no easement to import wastewater onto any downhill property,” he asserted. City Administrator Rosanna Bayon Moore has said that although the SB9 process is less transparent than what citizens are used to, City Hall is compelled to follow state law. “The Wistaria project is the first SB9 project in the City. SB9 overrides conventional local authority. The ministerial pathway intentionally removes local discretion, public noticing and participation from the equation. It is a major shift away from our approach to design review projects that involve neighborhood notification, engagement and oftentimes, compromise. Conformance with State law is the City’s obligation and we are actively seeking ways to improve community understanding of this new State framework,” she said. Members of the neighborhood voiced their opposition to the project at a City Council meeting on Monday, July 15. Nearly 30 residents attended the heated council meeting. “We’re here because the irreversible destruction of the property at 77 Wistaria Way is scheduled to start tomorrow if you do nothing,” began Harvey Lederman. “We’ve appeared now three times before you. Each time you’ve remained silent. We’ve had no reaction from this council.” Lederman also pushed back against the assertion that City Council’s hands were tied in the matter, adding that under section 54954.2A3 the Brown Act, City Council could direct their staff to suspend construction on Wistaria Way to give them more time to investigate the matter. That is, “if you had the will to do it,” he said. In addition to citizen comments, lawyer Rachel Doughty appeared via Zoom to represent a “group of neighbors who live nearby and in the general vicinity of this project.” “What we’re asking you to do tonight is something within your power,” she affirmed. The residents seemed to receive a show of empathy from Councilman Tom Ramsey, a former member of the Planning Commission, after public comment closed. “Can the city notify neighbors of SB9 applications?” he asked City Attorney Michelle Kenyon, who responded that the notification would serve “no purpose,” but that there is “nothing legally preventing the city from notifying residents about SB9 applications.” A brief set of questions and answers followed between council members Betsy Andersen, Ramsey, Conna McCarthy and Kenyon. Diane Prioleau, who has lived next door to the property since 1968, said she is worried about the precedent the action will set for nature and wildlife in Piedmont. “When they said there’s no creek on the property, I remembered my kids damming the stream when they were little and having a swimming hole,” she laughed. “It is a stream, and it is a creek. However, Prioleau took council members’ questions after the forum as a good sign for their cause. “It means we’re getting too big to be ignored.” For more information about the project on Wistaria Way, contact Planning Director Kevin Jackson in City Hall at 420-3050.

articles.text: The Troop 1 burger stand is a yearly tradition for nearly 30 years. Every Fourth of July, Troop 1 Scouts and their parents volunteer to run the stand. Some Scouts grill the burgers, others wrap them and the younger Scouts take orders from customers and work the registers. This is a good learning experience for the Scouting kids. Some of these Scouts only set foot in the kitchen at their homes to eat (me). Eagle Scouts Tobin and Alexander Cantrill stay busy at the Troop 1 burger stand grill. Scout Ayaan Jajodia cooking burgers. Scouts Sasha Liu and Ciaran Gallagher on July 4th. Scouts Theo Cost, Sammy Donnelly, and Susannah Cantrill helping customers at the Troop 1 Burger Stand. Now they can learn how to cook. Hopefully the burger stand will inspire them to cook more on their own. Scouts working at the Troop 1 burger stand get service hours while also helping the community. Piedmont Grocery has been the principal donor for many years, and The Grubb Co. has quietly helped fund the Scouts’ efforts. The food is also sourced from donations from Trader Joe’s, and Costco. Burgers were sold for $10 each, and this year there were four types – cheeseburger, regular burger, the impossible burger, and the impossible burger with cheese. The menu did not consist only of burgers. They also had watermelon slices and sparkling water. After getting a burger yummy condiments were are on the side of the stand, including lettuce, tomatoes, onions, ketchup, mustard, and pickles. Thanks to a lot of hungry people, Troop 1 Scouts earned around $5800 from four hours of work at the burger stand. All the profits go to funding future Scouting events. This subsidizes what Scouts have to pay for trips and events. Some of the money earned also goes to fund Eagle Scout projects in the future. Eagle Scout projects are the projects that current Scouts have to do to reach the rank of Eagle. These projects are required to help the community. For example, past projects were building a fence, doing an early project for the Piedmont Center for the Arts, and building benches. All of these projects benefit the community inside and outside of Piedmont. Remember, when you are supporting the Troop 1 burger stand, you are also funding Eagle Scout projects and making Piedmont and its surrounding area a better place. The Troop 1 burger stand is a great learning experience for Scouts, and has delicious food for parade participants and observers alike. Sasha Liu is a member of Troop 1 in the Piedmont Scout Council.
